:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=2$, and we get

$$
\int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{x^{3}}{3} + C) &=  \\
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{x^{3}}{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(C) &=  \\
\frac{1}{3}\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}) + 0 &=  \\
\frac{1}{3} \cdot 3x^{2} &=  \\
&= x^{2}✓
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We start by writing the square root as a rational power,

$$
\sqrt x= x^{1/2}
$$

So, we can apply the power rule with

$$
n=\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\sqrt{x}dx &= \intx^{1/2}dx \\
&= (x^{1/2 + 1})/((\frac{1}{2} + 1)) + C \\
&= (x^{3/2})/((\frac{3}{2})) + C \\
&= \frac{2x^{3/2}}{3} + C
\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3} + C) &=  \\
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(C) &=  \\
\frac{2}{3}\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3/2}) + 0 &=  \\
\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{2}x^{3/2 - 1} &=  \\
&= x^{1/2}✓
\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^3}$ and that $F'(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x)$.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if

$$
F'(x) = f(x)
$$

then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{′}(x) &= f(x) \\
\intF^{′}(x)dx &= \intf(x)dx \\
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

$$
\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}
$$

So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx \\
&= \int\frac{1}{x^{3}}dx \\
&= \intx^{-3}dx \\
&= \frac{x^{-3 + 1}}{-3 + 1} + C \\
&=-\frac{x^{-2}}{2} + C \\
&=-\frac{1}{2x^{2}} + C
\end{aligned}
$$
